summary: Return the values of the nodes visible from the right side, top to bottom.
mainInsight: The visible node on each level is its rightmost node. A level-order BFS takes the last node of every level; a DFS that visits the right child first and records the first node seen at each depth does the same.
canonicalApproach: BFS taking the last node of each level

approaches.name: BFS taking the last node of each level
approaches.summary: Snapshot the level; the last element is visible.

approaches.name: DFS right-first with a depth check
approaches.summary: Record the first value met at each new depth.

personalSolution.approach: BFS taking the last node of each level

promptVariants: What node of each level is visible from the right?
options: The last node of each level (BFS), or the first seen right-first (DFS)
The first node of the level, because it is closest to the root's left
The node with the largest value of the level, wherever it sits
The deepest leaf of the whole tree, since it is always visible
cards.answer: The last node of each level (BFS), or the first seen right-first (DFS)
cards.explanation: The right view contains the rightmost node of every level.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The deepest leaf of the whole tree, sinc: Only one node, not one per level.

promptVariants: Why is the right-side view not just the right spine?
How can a left child be visible?
cards.answer: If a level has no right-side node on the right spine (the right subtree is shorter), the rightmost node of a deeper level may be a left child, e.g. the deepest level belongs to the left subtree. Taking the last node per level handles that automatically.
cards.explanation: That is why BFS per level is the safe approach.

promptVariants: Compare the BFS and DFS space for the right side view.
Which of BFS and DFS is more memory-friendly for the right side view, and why?
cards.answer: BFS uses O(w) for the queue; right-first DFS uses O(h) for the recursion stack. The answer itself has one value per level.

promptVariants: Why do you check `queue[-1]` before processing the level and why the extra None checks?
cards.answer: At the start of a level the last element of the queue is that level's rightmost node, so its value is recorded before the level is consumed. The `if queue[-1]` guard exists because the initial queue may contain None for an empty tree; if only real nodes are ever enqueued, the extra `node and` checks are unnecessary after handling an empty root up front.
keyPoints: queue[-1] = rightmost node of the level
Guard only for an empty root

promptVariants: What is the right view of [1,2,3,null,4,5]?
cards.explanation: Level 2 holds 4 (under 2) and 5 (under 3, on its left): the rightmost node of the level is 5. In [1,2] the left child is visible because there is no right child.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[1,3,4] and [1,2]: 4 is hidden behind 5 on the same level, even though 5 is a left child.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[1,3,5] and [1]: With no right child, the left child 2 is the only node on its level, so it is visible.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[1,2,4] and [1]: 2 and 4 are on the left; the rightmost nodes of the levels are 3 and 5.
